cards.text: Meet Micah the Moreshite. The word of the LORD comes to him in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. And what he sees is about two cities: Samaria and Jerusalem.
Micah doesn't ease into this one. No small talk, no 'how's everybody doing,' he just opens with a call to HEAR and LISTEN.

cards.question: Micah opens with a call to listen. Who does he call to hear him?

answers.text: All peoples and the whole earth
The kings and priests of Judah
The elders and prophets of Israel

cards.text: He says, "May the Lord GOD bear witness against you, the Lord from His holy temple." Because look: the LORD comes forth from His dwelling place to come down and tread on the high places of the earth.

cards.question: When the LORD treads on the high places of the earth, what do the mountains beneath Him do?
While the mountains melt beneath the LORD, the valleys hold firm.

cards.text: So what's all this melting and splitting for? Micah says, "All this is for the transgression of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel."

cards.question: Micah asks, "What is the transgression of Jacob?" Which city does he point to?
Then Micah asks about the high place of Judah, and the city he names is ___.

cards.text: Now the LORD speaks, and friend, it's HEAVY. He'll make Samaria a heap of rubble in the open field, a planting area for a vineyard, with her stones poured into the valley and her foundations exposed.

cards.question: Along with the city itself, the LORD says He will destroy all of Samaria's ___.

cards.text: Her carved images get smashed to pieces, and her wages go into the fire. The LORD says, "Since she collected the wages of a prostitute, they will be used again on a prostitute."

cards.question: After hearing what's coming for Samaria, Micah says he will lament and wail.

cards.text: Micah says he'll walk barefoot and naked, howl like a jackal and mourn like an ostrich. When I got slid into that junk drawer, I just went quiet, but Micah lets it ALL out.

cards.question: Micah says Samaria's wound is incurable. How far has it spread?

cards.text: Now Micah's lament goes town by town. It starts with this: "Do not tell it in Gath; do not weep at all."

cards.question: Micah is mourning what's coming. What does he tell the people of Beth-leaphrah to do?

cards.text: Then Micah tells the dwellers of Shaphir to depart in shameful nakedness.
The dwellers of Zaanan will not come out. And Beth-ezel is in mourning.
The people of Maroth pined for good. But calamity came down, even to the gate of Jerusalem.

cards.question: The calamity that came down on Maroth came from the LORD.

cards.text: Next up, Lachish, and Micah has a command for it: "Harness your chariot horses, O dweller of Lachish."

cards.question: Micah says the transgressions of Israel were found in Lachish. He calls Lachish the beginning of ___ to the Daughter of Zion.

cards.text: Then Micah says to send farewell gifts to Moresheth-gath. That's the goodbye card the whole office signs.

cards.question: Micah says the houses of Achzib will prove dependable to the kings of Israel.
Then comes word for Mareshah. What is coming against Mareshah again?

cards.text: And the glory of Israel will come to Adullam. Then Micah's last call: shave yourselves bald, cut off your hair, and make yourselves as bald as an eagle.

cards.question: Why does Micah tell the people to shave themselves bald?

answers.text: To keep a vow to the LORD

cards.question: Micah says their precious children will go from them into ___.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's humor is thin across the whole walkthrough. There are only about four light moments: the small-talk line in stop 1 card 2, 'it's HEAVY' in stop 1 card 10, the junk drawer contrast in stop 1 card 14, and the office goodbye card in stop 2 card 9. None of them is a real laugh. Most story cards read like a pleasant narrator, not laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: Stop 2 cards 3, 4 and 5 are bare restatements of Micah 1:11-12 with no Papa Dorin voice at all. Examples: 'Then Micah tells the dwellers of Shaphir to depart in shameful nakedness.' and 'The dwellers of Zaanan will not come out. And Beth-ezel is in mourning.' Stop 1 cards 4 and 12 have the same problem.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The question itself says 'the transgressions of Israel were found in Lachish'. That rules out the wrong answers 'joy' and 'strength' before the baker reasons at all, so 'sin' is the only possible pick.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The question opens with 'Micah is mourning what's coming'. That setup rules out the wrong answer 'Dance in the streets', which leaves only two real choices.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Micah 1:10-15 is a town-by-town lament covering Gath, Beth-leaphrah, Shaphir, Zaanan, Beth-ezel, Maroth, Lachish, Moresheth-gath, Achzib, Mareshah and Adullam. The walkthrough gives it full story cards and four choice cards (stop 2 cards 2, 6, 8, 10 and 11). The long-stretch rule lists 'land boundaries and town lists' as stretches that get one summary card and no choice cards. It also says prophetic messages and speeches carry the heart of a passage and get full treatment.
findings.question: Does a prophetic lament built as a list of towns, like Micah 1:10-15, count as a long stretch (one summary story card, no choice cards), or as part of the prophet's message that gets story cards and choice cards like anything else?
